Adolescent fertility rates (ages 15–24) are displayed for six bins of youth labor force participation. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin, while the color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that labor-force-participation range.

</figcaption>

</figure>

Prelimary Analysis: This figure examines adolescents and highlights how literacy rates, labor force participation, and fertility rates jointly vary across groups. A notable pattern emerges in the lowest labor force participation bin: this group exhibits the lowest mean fertility rate but also the lowest literacy rate. One interpretation is that adolescents participating in the labor force at this stage may be entering forms of work that do not require or encourage formal schooling—such as informal or service-oriented jobs—leading to weaker literacy outcomes. Their lower fertility rate is consistent with the fact that adolescents who begin working may be older teens transitioning toward adulthood but not yet in the age range where fertility is highest.

Across the remaining labor force participation bins, mean fertility rates cluster around 20, but the range of fertility outcomes increases substantially at higher levels of labor force participation. In particular, the 33–40% bin shows the widest fertility range, followed by the subsequent two bins. This pattern suggests that adolescents in contexts with higher labor force participation may be entering the workforce at ages that coincide more closely with peak fertility windows. As a result, greater heterogeneity in fertility outcomes appears in these groups.

Interestingly, the highest labor force participation groups also show some of the highest fertility rates, which complicates the common assumption that fertility declines with increased female labor engagement. Instead, within this adolescent-focused context, higher labor force participation may reflect broader socioeconomic conditions—such as economic necessity or cultural norms—that simultaneously encourage early workforce entry and earlier childbearing. This highlights the importance of interpreting adolescent labor patterns within their social and economic environments, rather than assuming they mirror adult labor–fertility relationships.
